title: Next-hop troubleshooting
description: Investigate Lab 01’s wrong-mask fault, explain the next hop, then verify the repair. Review mistakes and apply each objective to a fresh scenario before earning an independent-application achievement.

objectives.label: Choose a test that distinguishes wrong addressing from a routing failure

achievement.title: Evidence before repair
achievement.reason: You chose a targeted addressing test in a new scenario without a hint or an incorrect attempt.

objectives.label: Use subnet comparison to distinguish the IP destination from the Ethernet next hop

achievement.title: Next hop explained
achievement.reason: You applied subnet and frame-address reasoning to a new scenario without assistance.

questions.title: A useful test before changing the network
questions.prompt: Lab 01: PC-A2 (192.168.10.11) can reach PC-A1 (.10), but not PC-B1 (.74). The approved Sales plan is /26, gateway .1; Ops is .64/26. A capture shows PC-A2 ARPing for .74 on LAN-A. Links and R1 connected routes are healthy; addresses are numeric, so DNS is not involved. Which check distinguishes a wrong host mask from a router fault?
questions.objective: Choose a test that distinguishes wrong addressing from a routing failure

choices.label: Compare PC-A2’s configured mask with the /26 plan before changing anything
choices.explanation: A /24 would incorrectly classify .74 as local, explaining the ARP target. Comparing configuration with the plan tests that explanation directly.

choices.label: Reboot R1 before checking host addressing
choices.explanation: Healthy connected routes and links make an untested router reboot weaker than inspecting the host decision that produced the ARP.

choices.label: Flush DNS and retry the numeric address
choices.explanation: The test uses numeric IPs; DNS lookup does not explain the observed on-link ARP for .74.

questions.hint: The ARP target tells you what PC-A2 believes is local. What host setting decides that?
questions.success: Test result: PC-A2 has /24. Restore the approved /26 (255.255.255.192), then verify; this is a scenario result, not a change to a real device.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: the return side fails
questions.prompt: New case: PC-B2 (192.168.10.75) reaches local .74 but cannot reply to PC-A1 (.10). It has gateway .65 and ARPs for .10 on Ops instead of forwarding to .65. The approved plan is Ops .64/26 and Sales .0/26. R1 and links are healthy. Which check distinguishes a mask error from a router fault?
questions.objective: Choose a test that distinguishes wrong addressing from a routing failure

choices.label: Inspect PC-B2’s mask against Ops’ /26 plan
choices.explanation: With /24, .10 would appear local; /26 makes it remote. Checking the host mask directly tests the observed incorrect on-link decision.

choices.label: Reset both switches’ MAC tables
choices.explanation: A switch forwards frames; clearing tables does not test why the host classified a remote IP as local.

choices.label: Change the destination IP to .65 so the same packet reaches PC-A1
choices.explanation: The destination IP must identify PC-A1. The gateway is the Ethernet next hop, not a replacement IP destination.

questions.hint: Determine which setting could make .75 and .10 appear on the same local network.
questions.success: Finding: the observed behavior is consistent with /24 on PC-B2. Confirm the configuration, repair to the approved /26, and retest both directions.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: a different address plan
questions.prompt: Authored transfer network: a host 10.20.0.10 should use /25 and gateway .1. Destination .150 is in 10.20.0.128/25. The host currently uses /24 and broadcasts ARP for .150; links and the router are healthy. Which test is justified before repair?
questions.objective: Choose a test that distinguishes wrong addressing from a routing failure

choices.label: Compare the configured /24 mask with the approved /25 plan
choices.explanation: The host’s /24 combines the two planned /25 networks. Comparing the mask explains why it wrongly ARPs for a remote host.

choices.label: Replace Ethernet with a faster NIC before testing the mask
choices.explanation: No link or capacity failure is given. A faster NIC does not change the host’s subnet comparison.

choices.label: Treat the three matching address octets as proof the destination is local
choices.explanation: Locality is determined by the mask, not simply by matching the first three octets.

questions.hint: The approved /25 boundary is .128; compare that boundary with the configured /24.
questions.success: The test supports repairing the mask to the approved /25 and checking routed delivery; the same principle applies to a different prefix.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Interpret the corrected next hop
questions.prompt: PC-A2 is now 192.168.10.11/26 with gateway .1. It sends to PC-B1 192.168.10.74/26. An ARP reply has resolved R1 Gi0/0 at .1. Which outbound address pairing is correct?
questions.objective: Use subnet comparison to distinguish the IP destination from the Ethernet next hop

choices.label: Destination IP .74; destination Ethernet MAC belongs to R1 Gi0/0 (.1)
choices.explanation: Subnet comparison puts .74 on Ops’ remote subnet. The IP packet still targets PC-B1; the local frame targets the gateway interface.

choices.label: Destination IP .1; destination MAC belongs to R1 Gi0/0
choices.explanation: Changing the destination IP to the gateway would address the router instead of PC-B1. Only the local frame’s next-hop address targets the gateway.

choices.label: Destination IP .74; destination MAC belongs to remote PC-B1 on LAN-A
choices.explanation: The remote host is not on this Ethernet segment. PC-A2 uses its local gateway’s MAC for the first frame.

questions.hint: Separate the end-to-end IP destination from the local Ethernet receiver.
questions.success: The first Ethernet hop reaches R1; R1 uses its connected Ops route and rebuilds the frame for PC-B1. Without NAT, the IP endpoints remain PC-A2 and PC-B1.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: reverse the direction
questions.prompt: New case: PC-B2 (.75/26) sends to PC-A1 (.10/26), gateway .65. Its ARP cache is initially empty. Which address should it resolve, and what IP destination should the packet retain?
questions.objective: Use subnet comparison to distinguish the IP destination from the Ethernet next hop

choices.label: Resolve .65’s MAC; retain destination IP .10
choices.explanation: PC-A1 is outside Ops .64/26, so the Ethernet next hop is R1 Gi0/1 at .65; the IP destination remains PC-A1.

choices.label: Resolve remote .10 directly on Ops; retain destination IP .10
choices.explanation: The remote host cannot answer ARP across the router. Resolve the on-link gateway instead.

choices.label: Resolve .65’s MAC; replace destination IP .10 with .65
choices.explanation: The gateway’s IP is used to resolve the local next hop; it is not the end-to-end destination.

questions.hint: Compare .75/26 and .10/26 before choosing an ARP target.
questions.success: The return direction uses a different gateway interface and local MAC, but the packet still addresses the intended remote host.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: keep local traffic local
questions.prompt: New case: PC-A1 (.10/26) sends to PC-A2 (.11/26). Both are on Sales, gateway .1. Its ARP cache is empty. Which local Ethernet delivery is justified?
questions.objective: Use subnet comparison to distinguish the IP destination from the Ethernet next hop

choices.label: Resolve .11’s MAC and keep destination IP .11
choices.explanation: Both hosts are within .0/26. ARP resolves the destination host locally; the gateway is not required for same-subnet delivery.

choices.label: Resolve .1’s MAC for every packet because a gateway is configured
choices.explanation: The host uses the gateway for remote destinations. A configured gateway does not make every frame traverse the router.

choices.label: Replace destination IP .11 with the switch management IP .2
choices.explanation: The switch forwards Ethernet frames; its management IP is not the packet’s intended destination.

questions.hint: A configured gateway does not override the local subnet comparison.
questions.success: The switch delivers the local frame toward PC-A2; no router hop is needed for this same-subnet path.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Verify and document the mask repair
questions.prompt: After restoring PC-A2 from /24 to the approved /26, what provides relevant evidence that the repaired path works? This is a small, controlled lab; successful ping proves IP reachability, not every application.
questions.objective: Verify the repaired path and document configuration and test results

choices.label: Check local, gateway and cross-subnet pings; record the corrected mask and results
choices.explanation: These checks separate local access, gateway access and the repaired remote path. Recording configuration and results documents what changed and what was actually verified.

choices.label: Close the ticket as soon as the mask is edited
choices.explanation: A configuration change is not proof of functionality. The remote path still needs to be tested and the result documented.

choices.label: Run only a same-subnet ping and declare remote delivery fixed
choices.explanation: Local delivery worked before the repair. It does not demonstrate that the previously failed cross-subnet path now works.

questions.hint: Repeat the previously failed path, not only a path that already worked.
questions.success: Scenario result: local, gateway and remote pings reply after ARP settles. Record .11/26, gateway .1, source/destination and results; application-specific checks remain separate.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: verify the reply path
questions.prompt: New case from Lab 01: PC-B2 (.75/26) lacked its default gateway, so local pings worked but remote replies failed. You restored gateway .65. Which verification and record best support closing this lab fault?
questions.objective: Verify the repaired path and document configuration and test results

choices.label: Test local and cross-subnet reachability in both directions; record .75/26, gateway .65 and results
choices.explanation: The missing gateway affected replies to another subnet. Testing the previously failed return path as well as local access and recording results checks the repair’s actual scope.

choices.label: Test only PC-B2 to local .74 because it is faster
choices.explanation: Local access worked before the gateway repair; it does not test the missing remote reply path.

choices.label: Record a reward score instead of the addressing and test results
choices.explanation: Practice points do not verify network functionality or document the configuration change.

questions.hint: The repaired setting was needed for remote replies. Which test exercises those replies?
questions.success: Successful lab pings support IP reachability in the tested directions. Record what was tested; do not generalize that every service works.

examMappings.area: Routing concepts (2.1), IPv4 addressing (1.7) and network troubleshooting methodology (5.1)

questions.title: Application: verify a router-interface repair
questions.prompt: Different Lab 01 fault: R1 Gi0/1 was administratively down and its Ops connected route disappeared. You applied no shutdown. Which checks and documentation verify this repair?
questions.objective: Verify the repaired path and document configuration and test results

choices.label: Confirm Gi0/1 up/up and the Ops connected route, then test cross-subnet pings and record results
choices.explanation: The repair must restore the interface and route as well as the formerly failed traffic path. Lab 01 documents show ip int brief, show ip route and cross-subnet pings for these purposes.

choices.label: Verify only that the no shutdown command was accepted
choices.explanation: Command acceptance does not prove interface state, route presence or successful forwarding.

choices.label: Clear host ARP caches and declare the interface repaired without traffic tests
choices.explanation: Cache changes do not establish that the interface or route is restored. Inspect the repaired components and exercise the failed path.

questions.hint: Verify the changed interface, the route it supplies, and the actual traffic path.
questions.success: The evidence is interface up/up, connected .64/26 via Gi0/1 and successful tested pings. Document the fault, change and observed results.

scenarios.title: Lab 01 · Sales and Ops
scenarios.description: Sales 192.168.10.0/26 → SW1 → R1 → SW2 → Ops 192.168.10.64/26. Questions explicitly state direction and any faulty configuration.
scenarios.assumptions: IPv4 over Ethernet; no NAT, VLAN changes or packet loss. ICMP is allowed. Lab addressing uses /26; every host has the stated gateway except an explicitly described fault. MAC addresses are authored diagram examples. ARP starts empty unless a resolved entry is stated. Initial IPv4 TTL is 64. Healthy links/routes are stipulated except the named interface fault.
context: All abbreviated node addresses share prefix 192.168.10. PC-A1 is .10/26; PC-B2 is .75/26. This diagram shows the approved plan, not a diagnosis of the current fault.
